title: Which letter appears the most in a news item?
description: A question from the book asks you to count five letters in a newspaper item and put them in order of frequency. The video gives the plan of tallying, reading, comparing and ordering, and says why most classmates get the same order.
teaching_notes: One idea: tally each letter while reading, read the counts, then order the letters from the smallest count to the largest. Watch for children who count words instead of letters or who skip a letter inside a long word.

source: Figure it Out: count the letters c, e, i, r and x in a news item and order them by frequency
video_script.why: The child runs the whole plan of collecting, counting and ordering on their own data and explains why classmates agree.
video_script.substitution: none: the question uses the child's own news item, so no counts are fixed
video_script.anchor: a small news item pasted on a sheet of paper, with a table of letters
video_script.payoff_line: Almost everyone gets the order ex, see, ar, eye, ee.

final_answer.value: x, c, r, i, e (e the most, x the least)
final_answer.spoken: almost everyone gets the order ex, see, ar, eye, ee, so ee is found the most and ex the least

maths_rules: The counts depend on the news item, so none is fixed.
Ascending order of frequency runs from the smallest count to the largest count.
The book says almost everyone gets the order x, c, r, i, e, with e the most and x the least.
video_script.design: A news item on a sheet, a table of the letters c, e, i, r and x with tally rows, and an ordered row of the five letters at the end.

beats.on_screen: title card with a small newspaper item pasted on a sheet, and the five letters c, e, i, r and x written beside it

marks.scene: the title card arrives with the sheet and the news item
marks.letters: the five letters light up one after another
marks.ask: a question mark lights up above the letters

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about a news item from a newspaper.
<bookmark mark='letters'/>You count five letters in its words: see, ee, eye, ar and ex.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which of these five letters will you meet the most?

beats.on_screen: the news item, the five letters and the question mark stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the news item with many letters, and an empty table with one tally row for each of the five letters

marks.many: the letters of the news item light up in many places
marks.plan: the empty table with its tally rows appears beside the item

narration: <bookmark mark='many'/>A news item holds many letters, so we need a plan for counting.
<bookmark mark='plan'/>We tally the letters one by one, and then read the counts.

beats.on_screen: Given: a small news item, and a table with the letters c, e, i, r, x and one more letter of your choice
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a small news item, and a table with a row for each of the five letters.

beats.on_screen: To find: the letter found the most, the letter found the least, and the five letters in ascending order of frequency

marks.find: the three lines to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the most, the least, and the order of the five letters.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: read the news item word by word and draw a tally mark in the right row for each letter

marks.read: a pointer moves along the words and a tally mark is added in the table each time one of the five letters is met

narration: <bookmark mark='read'/>Step one, read the news item word by word.
Each time you meet one of the five letters, draw a tally mark in its row.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: read each row of tally marks and write its count in the table

marks.count: each row is read as bundles of five and loose strokes, and its count is written in the last row of the table

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step two, read each row of tally marks and write its count.
Count every bundle as five, and then add the loose strokes.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: compare the counts: the largest count is the letter found the most, the smallest count is the letter found the least
narration: <bookmark mark='most'/>Step three, compare the counts in the table.
The largest count belongs to the letter found the most.
<bookmark mark='least'/>The smallest count belongs to the letter found the least.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: write the five letters from the smallest count to the largest, then compare your row with your classmates

marks.order: the five letters slide into a row from the smallest count to the largest
marks.compare: the row is placed beside the rows of classmates

narration: <bookmark mark='order'/>Step four, write the five letters from the smallest count to the largest.
<bookmark mark='compare'/>Then compare your row with the rows of your classmates.

beats.on_screen: Step 5: ask friends how they counted; the same plan works for another news item

marks.friends: two friends show their own ways of counting beside yours
marks.again: the same plan is applied to a new news item

narration: <bookmark mark='friends'/>Step five, ask your friends how they counted, and note their ways.
<bookmark mark='again'/>For another news item, the same plan works again.

beats.on_screen: Answer: almost everyone gets the order x, c, r, i, e; e is found the most and x the least

marks.ans: the answer row of five letters is boxed
marks.ends: the last letter of the row is circled for the most and the first letter for the least
marks.why: the same row of letters appears over several news items

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Almost everyone gets the order ex, see, ar, eye, ee.
<bookmark mark='ends'/>The letter ee is found the most, and ex is found the least.
<bookmark mark='why'/>English words use the letters in much the same proportions in any news item.
